title: Feng Xuan Buys Righteousness
text:
Lord Mengchang of Qi, in the 3rd century BC, kept thousands of retainers in his household. One of them, Feng Xuan, arrived poor and seemed to have no talents. The Strategies of the Warring States says he kept complaining by singing to his sword about having no fish to eat, no carriage and no means to support his mother, and Lord Mengchang provided each.

One day the lord needed someone to collect the debts owed to him by the people of his fief at Xue. Feng Xuan volunteered and asked what he should buy with the money. Lord Mengchang told him to buy whatever his household lacked. At Xue, Feng Xuan called together the debtors and checked their tallies. Then he announced, in his lord's name, that all the debts were forgiven, and he burned the tallies. The people cheered the lord's name.

Feng Xuan returned empty handed and explained that the lord's house had treasures, horses and beautiful women but lacked righteousness, so he had bought him some. Lord Mengchang was displeased.

A year later the king of Qi dismissed Lord Mengchang, and his retainers deserted him. He retired to Xue. While he was still a long way off, the people came out on the road, old and young, to welcome him. Lord Mengchang turned to Feng Xuan and said that now he saw the righteousness he had been bought.
lesson: Goodwill is an investment that pays when you need it most. Generosity given without immediate return can become your safest refuge.
source: Strategies of the Warring States (Zhanguo Ce), Strategies of Qi; also Sima Qian, Shiji, chapter 75 (as Feng Huan)
